Thank you for the opportunity to talk today about next of Kim Memorial Avenue. This is a national historic site.
Saskatoon is home to several national historic sites, some of which you may be familiar with.
The college building on campus now called the Peter McKinnon Building and the Forest of Farm Park and Zoo.
The Avenue leading to Woodland Cemetery known as Next of Kim Memorial Avenue is less well known. This is quite sad.
For those who are not familiar with it, this Avenue is lined with allen dreams, each of which is dedicated to a fallen soldier from the First World War.
It was in 1922 that the military chapter of the IOD proposed the planting of the Memorial Avenue.
It was part of the roads of remembrance movement that had started in Britain, an idea that spread across Canada.
The aim was to plant a living memorial, symbolizing victory of life over death.
The concept of a tree lined Avenue was also a reminder of those popular lined roads of northern France.
A mere one year later on June 17, 1923, the Avenue was dedicated before a crowd of 8,000 people.
On August 28, 1994, the Avenue received its designation as a national historic site.
The next of Kim Memorial Avenue is the only intact road of remembrance left in Canada.
Others have succumbed to disease and vandalism, but mostly they have succumbed to developmental pressure.
We are lucky indeed to have this national historic site intact within the city boundaries.
We are some well-known soldiers recognized along the Avenue.
Hugh Kerns, we see in his brother Albert, and Talmud Lawson, a co-owner of the then Sasquatoon daily star.
Last year, the Heritage Society received an inquiry from Belgium about a Belgian soldier who had a tree dedicated to him.
In June of this year, 2023, next of Kim Memorial Avenue will have reached its 100th birthday, a case of much pride and worthy of celebration.
We are asking the city to recognise this important anniversary and establish a committee to lead a discussion on how such a celebration can take place.
The Sasquatoon Heritage Society will be pleased to participate.
The city's cemetery master plan recognised the historic value of Wigland's cemetery and of Memorial Avenue.
It is also enthusiastic about promoting the history of the site.
What better way to do this than by holding a public celebration of the centennial of one of Sasquatoon's and Canada's important national historic sites?
